transcript:
[00:00] Ava (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — this is a deep dive on how we handle bursts and congestion control in the runtime, and practical knobs you can tune for Streamline's workload.
[00:18] Jenna (Streamline VP Eng): Hi all, thanks. We've been seeing tail latency spikes during morning batch windows, and costs are creeping up when we try to keep latency SLOs.
[00:29] Ravi (Redwood SE): Got it. We'll talk through the scheduler and batching tradeoffs — continuous batching usually helps throughput but can increase median latency for single-request paths unless you set guardrails.
[00:40] Marco (Streamline ML Infra): Quick Q: our workload has lots of short prompts (10-40 tokens) mixed with occasional 1k token requests. How do you avoid the long ones blocking the short ones?
[00:52] Liam (Redwood SE): Two levers: max_num_seqs (per-GPU concurrent sequences cap) and token limits per-request or per-route. If you allow long requests to join the same bucket as short requests, you get head-of-line blocking. We typically set a per-route token ceiling and a lower priority class for long-running sessions.
[01:12] Priya (SRE): When you say priority, is that preemption or queueing priority?
[01:18] Ravi: Queueing. We don't preempt in-flight token generation yet — that would require checkpointing the KV cache and is expensive. Instead we use slot-based priority windows: short/fast requests get smaller slots and higher scheduling weight. 
[01:33] Tom (CTO): Any impact on KV cache hit rate when splitting into priority lanes?
[01:38] Liam: Slightly. If you segregate traffic, the effective working set per lane shrinks, which can improve local KV hit for that lane, but you lose cross-request reuse. For Streamline's mix, we think a hybrid: keep a shared KV cache but have hot-route sticky slots so frequent short prompts get higher hit probability.
[01:58] Jenna: Can you explain continuous batching vs windowed packing with numbers?
[02:03] Ravi: Sure. Continuous batching attempts to form batches opportunistically as requests arrive, so you get smaller incremental latency but better throughput overall. Windowed packing accumulates for X ms then packs sequences tightly to maximize GPU utilization. Example: with continuous batching at our default settings you'll see 10-20% lower tail latency but maybe 5-15% lower max throughput than an aggressive 40ms window pack.
[02:27] Marco: So what's max_num_seqs do exactly?
[02:31] Liam: max_num_seqs controls the maximum number of concurrent sequences scheduled onto a single device/runloop. Raising it increases batching headroom and throughput but also increases memory pressure (KV cache and activations) and risk of longer scheduling stalls during straggler cleanup. We often benchmark at multiples: 128, 256, 512 depending on model size and quantization.
[02:52] Priya: You mentioned quantization — how much does that change safe max_num_seqs?
[02:57] Ravi: Quantization like NF4 or int8 reduces memory per token so you can push max_num_seqs up 1.5x to 2x before hitting OOM, but int8 can increase compute time slightly on some kernels. The tradeoff is cost vs latency. For a 13B model, NF4 might let you go from 256 to 384 seqs; for an 70B it might only be 128->160. These are rough, we need bench numbers.
[03:22] Tom: What about token caps per request — we want to allow occasional long conversations for power users but not impact everyone.
[03:28] Liam: Configurable per-route token ceilings are the practical approach. Also set "burst tokens" — a small overage allowance for authenticated premium routes that borrow tokens from a reserve bucket. That way long-running sessions are rate-limited but allowed.
[03:41] Jenna: How do you smooth burst load when we get sudden spikes? We get 10x traffic for a minute during feature releases.
[03:47] Ravi: Two things: short-term burst smoothing via token buckets at the API edge + adaptive window expansion at the scheduler. If the scheduler sees a sudden spike, it temporarily relaxes packing thresholds to absorb extra seqs, then drains. For sustained spikes, autoscaler/ Dedicated reservation should be used.
[04:05] Marco: Does that mean we need dedicated capacity? We were hoping private VPC could be enough.
[04:10] Ava: Private VPC works, but autoscaling there depends on your infra. If you have strict latency SLOs during peaks, reserved capacity (Dedicated) or pre-warmed nodes are safest. For VPC on-prem, we can recommend an autoscaler config and a buffer pool.
[04:24] Priya: Network becomes a concern for us on-prem — how does RPC latency and bandwidth affect batching?
[04:29] Ravi: High egress latency hurts continuous batching because per-request arrival jitter increases. Also, if your nodes are multi-host, inter-GPU NVLink/RDMA vs Ethernet matters. We recommend colocated GPUs with fast interconnect for best packing. For VPC, ensure MTU and flow control are tuned and that we have predictable network paths to the control plane.
[04:49] Jenna: Could you share a simple knob set for our workload to try during pilot?
[04:53] Ava: Yes, we'll share presets. Off the top: max_num_seqs=256 for your 13B baseline with NF4, request_token_limit=1024 for public routes, premium_token_burst=2048 with rate decay, continuous_batch_low_latency=true, window_ms_peak=30. We'll put exact numbers in the spreadsheet after we see your traces.
[05:12] Marco: On KV cache eviction, what's recommended? LRU? TTL-based?
[05:17] Liam: We typically use frequency-weighted LRU with route stickiness. TTL helps for some long conversations but isn't great for small repeated prompts. Eviction tuning correlates strongly with hit-rate; if hit-rate drops below ~60% you lose most of the benefit. We'll show you a heatmap of hit-rate vs slot size in the bench sheet.
[05:36] Priya: How do we measure effective hit-rate? What metrics should we collect?
[05:40] Ravi: Collect per-route kvcache_hits, kvcache_misses, avg_seq_len, avg_tokens_per_minute, scheduler_queue_lat_p50/p95, batch_fill_ratio, and GPU_mem_util. Also track tail latency (p99) per-route.
[05:54] Tom: Any gotchas for quantization and dispatch kernels? We run some custom ops in the model.
[06:00] Liam: Custom ops can break optimized kernels; we need to ensure they run in the same compute path. If custom kernels are CPU-only you might see a GPU stall while copying; better to host ops on device or encapsulate them as fused ops. We'll checklist that for the pilot.
[06:16] Jenna: Let's dig into a concrete scenario — 2k qps of 20-token requests with 5% of 1k token requests interleaved. How to avoid head-of-line?
[06:26] Ravi: Recommended: create two priority lanes — lane A (short) with max_num_seqs_per_device=300 and tight token cap 256, lane B (long) with max_num_seqs_per_device=80 and token cap 4096. Shared KV cache with sticky routing for repeat sessions. Also use aggressive eviction for lane B to avoid polluting lane A's working set.
[06:47] Marco: Do lanes increase scheduling overhead?
[06:50] Liam: Slightly, but the scheduler is optimized for multiple pools. The overhead is minor compared to the gains in latency isolation.
[06:58] Ava: I'll pause to share a link to the benchmark doc we use for similar mixes — (link) https://redwood-internal/bench/presets/short-long-mix — note this is internal, will share sanitized copy.
[07:12] Marco: There's a bit of background noise — sorry about that.
[07:15] Priya: (laughs) all good.
[07:18] --- [skipping ahead as we walk through a sample benchmark table] ---
[25:10] Ravi: Looking at baseline numbers, with continuous batching and max_num_seqs=256 we see throughput 75k tokens/s and p95 latency 240ms; raising to 384 increases throughput 25% but p95 rises to 420ms. If you need firm p95 below 300ms, stay at 256 and add a small dedicated buffer pool.
[25:34] Jenna: Can Redwood help run this profiling on our infra?
[25:37] Ava: Yes, for the pilot we run a controlled load generator against your VPC deployment and collect the same metrics. We also provide a recommended autoscaler config.
[25:47] Marco: For the pilot, do you need admin access? We prefer scoped roles.
[25:52] Liam: Scoped service account with kube-admin-ish permissions for namespace level is enough. We'll detail required minimal RBAC in the checklist.
[26:02] Priya: Security — we need SOC2 docs and SAML SSO integration notes.
[26:06] Ava: We'll send SOC2 Type II and a SAML integration guide after the call.
[26:11] Tom: In terms of fallback strategies — if the cluster is saturated, what happens to requests?
[26:17] Ravi: We have layered fallbacks: 1) graceful degrade via token ceilings (shorten responses), 2) route-level fallback to a cheaper smaller model, 3) hard reject with a friendly 429 if nothing else. Fallback ordering is configurable per-route.
[26:30] Marco: How do you measure regression risk when using smaller models as fallback?
[26:34] Liam: We recommend a canary evaluation dataset. Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and raise alerts if quality drops below thresholds. We'll include suggested eval sets for your top 10 prompts.
[26:47] Jenna: Any network or VPC-specific tuning for our cloud provider?
[26:51] Ravi: Make sure health checks are configured to avoid flapping nodes, tune keepalive and TCP buffer sizes for high throughput, and if possible enable ENA or enhanced networking. For on-prem, ensure jumbo frames and RDMA where available.
[27:05] Priya: Will the pilot require dedicated GPUs?
[27:08] Ava: You can start on shared nodes but for strict SLOs we recommend reserving 1-2 full GPUs as buffer for burst absorption. We'll show sizing guidance.
[27:18] Marco: Are there any quick wins we can try with config changes only, before pilot?
[27:22] Ravi: Yes: lower window_ms from 40->20 to reduce tail latency, set token_limit per route, enable sticky KV for top routes, and set a conservative max_num_seqs. These are safe and reversible.
[27:35] Jenna: Sounds good. What's a realistic timeline to get pilot metrics?
[27:38] Ava: Once we have traces and infra access, 1 week to run a baseline and a tuned run, then another week for a burn-in. So 2-3 weeks end-to-end.
[27:48] --- [brief side discussion about billing model and reserved capacity pricing — omitted] ---
[34:05] Ravi: A couple of deep notes: when you raise max_num_seqs, watch out for scheduler GC pauses when cleaning very long sequences. We instrument a concurrent cleanup that uses amortized CPU, but spikes can still appear if lots of long requests finish simultaneously. Spreading long requests across time windows helps.
[34:25] Marco: Is there telemetry we can add to detect such GC spikes automatically?
[34:29] Liam: Yes — track scheduler_gc_duration, active_long_seq_count, and batch_eviction_events. We can add alerts if GC > 200ms more than N times/min.
[34:43] Jenna: For our compliance team, can we get a simple network diagram of the VPC flow?
[34:48] Ava: Yes, we'll attach a standard VPC checklist and a diagram for the private control plane.
[34:55] Priya: Any recommendations on model quantization strategy during pilot? We have a mix of production and experimental models.
[35:01] Ravi: Start by quantizing a non-critical model to NF4 and measure. If quality is acceptable, move a portion of traffic. For critical paths, keep fp16 or bf16. We'll provide a script to compare logits and a quality delta metric.
[35:15] Tom: One more operational question — can routing fallback be regional? If one region gets toasted we want to route to another region's dedicated pool.
[35:22] Liam: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based regional failover with automatic model variant fallback. There's a cross-region replication of warm caches we can enable but it increases network replication cost. We'll discuss tradeoffs for you.
[35:37] Jenna: OK wrapping up — let's confirm next steps.
[35:40] Ava: Next steps recap: share presets + bench sheet, you upload traces, Redwood prepares pilot plan and minimal RBAC steps, and we'll target week of 7/21 for pilot kickoff.
[35:52] Marco: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[36:00] --- [end of main session, casual closeouts and microtalk] ---
[57:30] Ava: Thanks all — logs will be shared and we'll follow up with action items.
[57:38] Jenna: Thank you.
